destinations.name: Moon
destinations.subtitle: Earth's Moon

objective.title: Map water ice in polar craters
objective.explain: Future astronauts will need water. Find where ice hides in dark craters near the poles.

destinations.fact: Some craters near the Moon's poles have not seen sunlight for billions of years. They are colder than Pluto and may hold water ice.

window.note: The Moon is close: you can launch almost any month.

orbits.name: Flyby
orbits.summary: Fly past once. Cheapest, but only a few hours of close-up science.
orbits.explain: The spacecraft swings past and keeps going. No braking needed, so no extra fuel.

orbits.name: Orbiter
orbits.summary: Circle the Moon for years and map all of it.
orbits.explain: The main engine brakes so the Moon's gravity captures the spacecraft. That braking fuel adds about 50% to the mass.

orbits.name: Lander
orbits.summary: Touch down inside one crater. Close look, but only one spot.
orbits.explain: No air on the Moon, so engines must brake all the way down: lots of fuel. The lunar night lasts 14 Earth days at −170 °C, so solar landers freeze.

realMission.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)
realMission.text: LRO maps the whole Moon from a low polar orbit. Its radar, cameras and spectrometers found signs of ice in dark polar craters, and it has kept working for more than 15 years.
realMission.lesson: An orbiter sees the whole Moon. A lander sees one crater.

destinations.name: Mars
destinations.subtitle: The Red Planet

objective.title: Find signs of ancient water
objective.explain: Mars once had rivers and lakes. Find the minerals and landforms that water left behind.

destinations.fact: Orbiters found clay minerals on Mars that only form in water. Billions of years ago, Mars had rivers, lakes and maybe an ocean.

window.note: Earth and Mars line up well only once every 26 months. Launch outside that window and the trip needs much more fuel.

orbits.name: Flyby
orbits.summary: Fly past once. Cheapest, but only a few hours of close-up science.
orbits.explain: The spacecraft swings past Mars and keeps going around the Sun. No braking fuel needed.

orbits.name: Orbiter
orbits.summary: Circle Mars for years. Sees the whole planet, good link to Earth.
orbits.explain: The main engine brakes for about 25 minutes so Mars can capture the spacecraft. That fuel adds about 60% to the mass.

orbits.name: Lander
orbits.summary: Land on the surface. Touch the rocks, but only one place. Needs a heat shield.
orbits.explain: Mars has thin air: a heat shield and a parachute do most of the braking, rockets do the rest. Without a heat shield the spacecraft burns up.

realMission.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO)
realMission.text: MRO carries a powerful camera (HiRISE), a mineral spectrometer and a ground-penetrating radar. Its 3-meter high-gain antenna has sent home more data than any earlier Mars mission.
realMission.lesson: Science only counts when it reaches Earth. That's why MRO has a big antenna.

destinations.name: Europa
destinations.subtitle: Icy moon of Jupiter

objective.title: Study the ice shell and hidden ocean
objective.explain: Under Europa's ice there is probably a salty ocean. How thick is the ice? Is the ocean really there?

destinations.fact: Europa's hidden ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

window.note: Earth and Jupiter line up well about once every 13 months.

orbits.name: Flyby tour
orbits.summary: Orbit Jupiter and swoop past Europa again and again, like Europa Clipper.
orbits.explain: Each pass is short, then the spacecraft escapes Jupiter's deadly radiation to cool off and send data home. Braking into Jupiter orbit still needs fuel.

orbits.name: Orbiter
orbits.summary: Circle Europa itself. Best view, but you live inside the radiation.
orbits.explain: Jupiter's radiation belts fry electronics. Orbiting Europa means staying in them, so the mission lasts months, not years. Lots of braking fuel too.

orbits.name: Lander
orbits.summary: Land on the ice. Huge science, huge risk.
orbits.explain: No air, extreme radiation and a very long trip. The lander needs the most fuel of all and lasts only weeks.

realMission.name: Europa Clipper
realMission.text: Launched on a heavy rocket, it reaches Jupiter in 2030 and will fly past Europa 49 times instead of orbiting it, to limit radiation damage. Its electronics sit in a thick-walled vault, and its solar arrays are over 30 meters wide.
realMission.lesson: Many short flybys beat one long stay when radiation is the enemy.
